Eighteen people were crushed to death in Xining, capital of Qinghai province, when 100,000 people who turned out to watch a lantern procession panicked, the official New China News Agency said today. 
Seven people were trampled to death in Lankao county, Henan province, as a crowd of 20,000 dispersed after watching a fireworks show, it said.

The building toppled into a river beside the construction site while the men were asleep at midnight Monday, and the sole survivor was found clinging to a log floating in the water.

The People's Daily newspaper said the survivors managed to climb out the rear window, while the rest of the 83 people on board burned to death. 
The bus crashed Wednesday in a rural area of Shaanxi Province in northern China, the paper said.

A ferry carrying at least 232 people to a popular south China tourist area capsized today during an overnight thunderstorm, leaving at least 147 people missing and feared dead, officials said.
Officials in Guangdong Province said the ferry was on its regular run from Canton, the province capital, to Zhaoqing, 46 miles to the west, when winds heeled it sharply to port and capsized it at 2:40 A.M.
Most of the passengers were believed to have been asleep and had little time to grab life preservers before the boat turned over in a river called the Shan Shui.
PEKING, March 1 (UPI) - A ferry carrying at least 232 people to a popular south China tourist area capsized today during an overnight thunderstorm, leaving at least 147 people missing and feared dead, officials said.
Nearly 24 hours after the disaster, officials said only 85 people had been rescued with 66 of them requiring hospitalization. 
At least 147 people were missing.

file: CHINA BELIEVED TO HAVE UNDERSTATED SCALE OF DROUGHT AND FLOOD DISASTERS.txt
text:
ï»¿
Chinese leaders apparently decided late last fall to deliberately understate the dimensions of China's drought and flood calamities in making their first appeal for international relief aid in more than 30 years. 
They are reported to have acted out of fear of alarming donor nations, antagonizing other third world disaster victims and damaging domestic political stabilityI.
According to Chinese officials, Western diplomats and relief workers here, the Peking leadership decided after ''sensitive'' debates to limit their aid appeal to apply only to hard-hit provinces containing about 21 million seriously affected victims of drought and flood because the dimensions of the overall problems were ''too big.''
International relief officials and some Western diplomats estimate that more than 130 million people are facing varying degrees of food shortages in at least nine provinces. 
But they are quick to stress that people are not starving and that the Government's own relief effort is well under way and seems fairly well organized.
Chinese leaders make first appeal for international relief aid in 30 years following country's severe drought and flood disastersNot Like Africans' Plight
''While we are talking about enormous areas and enormous numbers of affected people, China's problems should in no way be compared to the death and starvation among refugees in Africa,'' said a relief worker with experience in both places. 
''There is malnutrition, and some of it is serious and getting more serious. 
There are diseases growing out of it. 
But there is food to guarantee survival, and the Chinese are handling the bulk of the problems themselves with varying degrees of effectiveness.''
Perhaps to underscore the contrast with Africa, earlier this month at a Geneva conference China pledged $1 million to the relief effort for African refugees. 
The pledge was made despite an estimate by a United Nations survey team in March that China would need $700 million in food and other aid for disaster victims in Hebei and Hubei Provinces alone.
Hebei Province encircles Peking and is centered in the north China plain, which Chinese officials have said is into its second year with little or no rain. 
They said the drought is the region's worst in 38 years. 
Parts of at least seven provinces are affected: Liaoning, Hebei, Shanxi, Shaanxi, Ningxia, Gansu and Inner Mongolia.
The meterological bureau reported that between .12 and .8 of an inch of rain fell on parts of this region on April l3 and 14, helping the winter wheat crop planted last fall, but not by much.
Hubei Province in central China was the most seriously hit by torrential rains and subsequent flooding of the Yangtze River last summer. 
The Yangtze crested at its highest level in 26 years. 
To protect cities along the river, including Wuhan, Nanjing and Shanghai, workers hastily broke dozens of embankments along feeder rivers. 
Other burst themselves, inundating rural but heavily populated areas in Hubei and Anhui Provinces.
Chinese officials told the United Nations survey team that 550 people had died in the flooding and that about 41,000 had been injured. 
Whole villages were swept away, as were grain and vegetable crops and farm animals. 
Much land is too waterlogged to grow anything this year, they said.
Â 
Grain Stockpiles Dwindling
Relief officials said the drought in the north was most worrisome because no end to it is in sight and communal and district stockpiles of grain and other food harvested in previous years are rapidly dwindling. 
Reservoirs and rivers have dried up, and the water table in some areas has dropped to the point where villagers cannot dig emergency wells without modern deep-drilling equipment, which is in short supply.
Emergency rations of coarse grains, mainly ground corn, are being distributed, along with some dried cabbage and radishes. 
These provide between 1,200 and l,500 calories per day per person, several hundred calories short of minimum daily requirements of sustenance and child growth. 
Relatives living outside affected regions have been sending or bringing food in as well.
Before quietly approaching the United Nations last November, Chinese officials carefully weighed both the international and domestic political consequences of seeking foreign relief aid. 
Their decision to go ahead involved reversing to some extent a policy of self-reliance that has been a source of propaganda and pride since 1949.
Â 
Self-Reliance Still Stressed
When the United Nations disaster relief co-ordinator announced on March 12 that his organization would open an international appeal on behalf of China, he noted Peking's declaration that self-reliance continues to be a ''basic principle.''
At a news conference on March 31, Du Runsheng, deputy minister in the State Agricultural Commission, said that ''China has always undertaken our obligations'' financially to international organizations such as the United Nations but that in the past China had ''waived its right to benefit.''
He said China viewed its participation as a ''two-way street'' and ''strictly a question of mutual help.''
Mr. Du said the international aid China was seeking was small compared with the country's needs and that the domestic relief effort ''far exceeds'' whatever outside donors will contribute.
Â 
Possibilities for Aid Limited
Some Western diplomats interpreted China's limited request for aid as an effort not to scare away donor nations that might view the dimensions of China's needs as overwhelming. 
They also say that China does not want to antagonize its political friends in the third world that are suffering from their own disasters and are highly conscious that the amount of international relief aid is limited.
While the numbers of people affected seem enormous and while there are ample cases of serious malnutrition and disease, relief officials point out that all numbers in China seem enormous and that distinguishing victims of natural disaster from people affected by the poverty stemming from what the Chinese call man-made disasters is often difficult.
Relief workers believe that one reason the Chinese Government limited their inspections to two provinces is that the officials are loath to allow foreigners to document the effect of the admittedly disastrous consequences of China's agricultural policies over the last quarter-century.
Heavy commune building, central planning that ignored local conditions, tree-cutting and subsequent erosion, misguided irrigation projects causing saline buildup in soil and other policies that are now discredited left hundreds of millions of Chinese peasants with nothing to show for 25 years of toil.
Statistics compiled in the February issue of the magazine Economic Management imply that there were millions of unaccounted-for deaths between 1957, the beginning of the Great Leap Forward, and 1960, which began a period of famine.
Â 
Millions Lack Enough to Eat
At a Communist Party work conference in April 1979, Deputy Chairman Li Xiannian was reliably reported to have said that about 100 million people in China did not have enough to eat. 
That was before the current droughts and last year's floods.
Foreign pledges of aid for China have been trickling in. 
Emergency United Nations shipments of vitamins have arrived and are being distributed to supplement emergency grain rations. 
The European Common Market pledged $6.2 million worth of powdered milk and rapeseed oil along with other food supplies. 
Japan has pledged powdered milk as well.
The Peking leadership, meanwhile, faces a double-edged domestic sword as a consequence of its appeal for outside aid. 
Diplomats say if China discloses the full extent of its needs, it faces domestic criticism for failing at self-reliance. 
If it does not, foreign responses might be embarrassingly small and Mr. Deng's critics could use that as another example of the failure of his cooperation with non-Communist countries.

The State Council, China's Cabinet, dismissed Forestry Minister Yang Zhong today, saying he bore responsibility for a huge forest fire that killed 191 people and charred a huge area of northeastern China, the official New China News Agency said.
The fire, in Heilongjiang Province on the Soviet border, injured 221 people, left 51,000 homeless, destroyed several villages and burned more than 2.47 million acres.
The decision to dismiss Mr. Yang, 55 years old, will be submitted to the standing committee of the National People's Congress for approval, the agency said. 
No replacement was immediately named.
The dismissal indicated displeasure with the announced cause of the fire -carelessness by Forestry Bureau employees - and efforts to extinguish it.

China's populous southeastern province of Guangdong has begun recovering from severe floods that marooned 450,000 people and left at least 430 dead.
The floods, said to be the worst in Guangdong in 30 years, came after torrential rains early May 12. 
They affected over a million people in northern and western Guangdong and raised fears that Canton might be threatened.
PEKING, May 19 - China's populous southeastern province of Guangdong has begun recovering from severe floods that marooned 450,000 people and left at least 430 dead.
Today, People's Daily, in its first acknowledgment of the disaster, reported that the floodwaters were starting to recede and that stranded people were being evacuated. 
The official party newspaper did not say how many Chinese had died or been left homeless.
Fuller details, however, have appeared in the Hong Kong press, which reported on the casualties, and in a local newspaper, Canton's Yangcheng Evening News, copies of which reached Peking.
In Qingyuan County, less than 50 miles north of Canton, nearly 24 inches of rain fell in 13 hours, raising the North River to its highest level since 1949 and leaving some roads six feet under water. 
More than 4,000 soldiers and peasants were mobilized to reinforce the river's dikes.
Â 
46,000 Houses Collapse
The floodwaters inundated more than 286,000 acres of farmland, according to reports. 
The Yangcheng Evening News said 46,000 houses collapsed and 40 bridges were washed away along with telephone poles and smaller dikes. 
One account said Qingyuan and Yingde Counties were entirely under water. 
In all, 18 counties were affected.
The floods also swept away more than 20 miles of the main rail line between Canton and Peking. 
Rail traffic is not expected to be restored for two weeks, a local official said. 
Travelers arriving in Hong Kong reported being stranded on trains for 30 hours as the waters rose and landslides blocked the tracks.
Chinese television this week showed army units rescuing stranded peasants, some from rooftops. 
Military aircraft dropped tons of biscuits, clothing and candles. 
Helicopters also evacuated some people. 
Sailors in landing craft and rubber dinghies rescued others. 
More than 100,000 troops and civilians have been mobilized, according to one report.
The flood's effect has been felt in Hong Kong, where food prices jumped this week after the usual supplies of pork and vegetables were disrupted. 
Daily vegetable shipments from Guangdong dropped by more than a third over the weekend, and the Hong Kong authorities started ordering extra produce from Taiwan and Thailand.
Guangdong Province, whose population of 58 million exceeds that of Britain or France, is primarily agricultural, and the full impact of the devastation probably will not be known for some time.
Â 
Drought in Northern China
Other parts of Guangdong had floods last fall but recovered sufficiently to have a good harvest. 
The latest floods appear to be less severe than those in Sichuan and Shanxi Provinces last summer, when more than 1,000 Chinese were reported killed and up to a half million were left homeless.
Northern China, meanwhile, is having a drought. 
The authorities say Peking's water reserves are dangerously low, although rain in the last week has helped.
Guangdong's flood relief effort is being led by Yang Deyuan, a Deputy Governor. 
Li Xuan, a Deputy Minister of Railways, came from Peking to supervise the restoration of China's north-south trunk line. 
China's airline has sent extra planes to Canton to carry passengers and mail.
The New China News Agency, said Tuesday night in its first report on the flood, ''The water levels of rivers have been falling slowly in the past two days and surface water is subsiding.''
And in the province of Qinghai, People's Daily reported today, heavy spring snows last month killed 690,000 head of livestock.

file: Flash Floods and Drought Ravage China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Flash flooding along China's eastern coast has killed thousands of people and left tens of thousands homeless so far this year, and a drought in the country's central and southern grain belts has damaged millions of acres of crops.
Over the last four days, more than 200 people have died and 450 more were listed as missing in floods that engulfed parts of the coastal province of Zhejiang, news reports said.
At the same time, a heat wave continues to grip the Chinese heartland, from Jiangsu Province, across Anhui and Hubei Provinces, and into Jiangxi Province. 
Officials say 65 million acres of grain have been devastated by temperatures of 100 degrees and higher.
More than one-fifth of China's 296 million acres of farmland have been hurt by drought this year, with 24 million acres damaged by floods.
Natural disasters are a common feature of life in China, and their effect is accentuated by poorly constructed homes, bridges and dams; inadequate flood-control devices, and rudimentary road networks in rural areas - all of which hamper rescue efforts.
This year, the effect of the flooding and the heat wave is more severe, and many Chinese speak fatalistically about the cataclysms that every 12 years seem to accompany the Year of the Dragon.
''It's the dragon year,'' said a man who returned from Hebei Province on Sunday. 
''In 1976, there was the big earthquake, and the Chairman died,'' he said, speaking of the previous Year of the Dragon, when a catastrophic earthquake in Tangshan killed 100,000 people, and Mao Zedong died.
So far this year, a combination of floods, drought, landslides and cold spells have killed 11,588 people, destroyed 470,000 houses and affected the lives of 64 million people, a report in the English-language China Daily said.
Five counties in the central part of Zhejiang Province have been struck by flash floods, said The People's Daily, the official newspaper of the Communist Party. 
In a torrential rainstorm on July 29 and July 30, the paper said, nearly 700 people were reported missing, almost 17,000 houses were destroyed, the banks of 100 reservoirs crumbled, and 305 bridges collapsed.
China's central television station showed scenes of devastation, including towns with flooded streets. 
Fallen trees and other debris were shown sweeping past crumbling houses in a muddy torrent. 
Troops were sent to the region.
Â 
Oil Wells and Granaries
Meanwhile, Heilongjiang Province was battered by severe rain and hailstorms that affected 40 percent of the farmland in that northeastern region, The People's Daily said. 
Half the cities and counties in the province were struck by the storms, which flooded 1,000 oil wells and inundated grain stores, factories, shops and schools.
In the south and center of China, a stubborn heat wave parched paddy fields and withered rice stalks, damaging or destroying large portions of the year's first crop.
Officials in Hubei, one of the provinces hardest hit by the drought, reported that more than half the arable land in the region shriveled under the absense of rain and that two-thirds of the peanut and sesame crops were lost for the year.
''The drought is not only happening here in China,'' said Fan Yongxiang, the chief meteorologist at the Central Meteorological Bureau. 
''It's a global one.''
Mr. Fan suggested two possible causes for the dry spell. 
The first was an increase in sunspot activity earlier in the summer. 
Sunspots, which run in 11-year cycles, lead to strong electro-magnetic disturbances on earth.
The other was the global increase in temperatures attributed substantially to the greenhouse effect, in which an excess of carbon dioxide and other gases, produced primarily by the burning of carbon-based fuels, collects in the atmosphere, trapping heat and causing a gradual warming of the planet. 
Although the greenhouse effect's functioning has yet to be definitively established, there is a consensus among specialists that it is the cause of hotter temperatures on earth.
A spokesman for the Chinese Agriculture Ministry said the drought is the second this year in the region. 
The first occurred in April and May.
Xu Yuchang, a spokesman for the relief department of the Ministry of Civil Affairs, said more than 1 billion yuan, or about $270 million, has been allocated for relief work in drought- and flood-stricken areas. 
Mr. Xu said that families were being moved from flooded areas but that it was too early to say how many people were affected.
Last week, the United States Department of Agriculture said that China had bought 400,000 metric tons of wheat at subsidized prices.
In the last two years, the United States has exported seven million tons of wheat to China, according to the official New China News Agency. 
Some grain traders in Beijing today expressed doubts about whether China could achieve its stated grain-production goal of 410 million tons this year.
